newsitem.title: UK: FEATURE - Oscar nominee Fiennes hailed as new Olivier.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Oscar nominee Fiennes hailed as new Olivier.

text.p: Steven Spielberg told Ralph Fiennes he could be the next Laurence Olivier if he didn't forget his theatrical roots.

Britain's new screen heart-throb certainly took the advice to heart. Feted by Hollywood, nominated this year for an Oscar, he has come home to perform Chekhov's "Ivanov" at a tiny London fringe theatre for just 200 pounds ($320) a week.

Tortured souls are his speciality, from the sadistic Nazi officer in Spielberg's "Schindler's List" to the love-lorn Hungarian count in "The English Patient", which has won 12 Oscar nominations including Best Actor for Fiennes.
In between came an award-winning Hamlet in London and on Broadway from an actor torn in his private life between loyalty and love.
The 34-year-old abandoned Alex Kingston, his sweetheart from drama student days, after falling in love with 52-year-old Francesca Annis who played Hamlet's mother, Gertrude.
"She seems unnaturally fond of her son, caressing and kissing him with a warmth that would make Freud straighten up and polish his glasses," one critic wrote.
The fiercely private Fiennes bridles at interviewers more interested in his love life. He resents the intrusion and quickly switches to talk about his stagecraft.

You may even get treated lightheartedly to the "Rafe Lecture." He patiently explains that his name which is pronounced Ralph Fiends (rpt Fiends) in America should be pronounced Rafe Fines to rhyme with Safe Lines.
FIENNES REVELLED IN COMPLEXITY OF SCREEN CHARACTER

At the London premiere of "The English Patient," Fiennes talked of the joys of filming in the Tunisian desert -- director Anthony Minghella regarded it as a nightmare -- and the horrors of being transformed into a burns victim.

"I loved the desert," he told Reuters. "There is something about the stillness, the openness and the light in the desert. The shapes of the sand, the rocks, it is poetic, it is hypnotic. I find it a peaceful and very soothing place."

He revelled in the complexity of his character, Count Almasy: "It is a very rich mix. That was the attraction." Minghella said Fiennes telephoned and said he wanted to do the film. "It took me about 1/4 of a second to say 'yes'". Fiennes had to go through six hours in make-up before he could take to the set covered from head to toe in burned tissue.
"People looked at me very oddly when I had the make-up on. It was a mixture of horror and compassion. It was peculiar how it affected people. Some couldn't even talk to me."
Despite the Oscar nomination, Fiennes is wary of being sucked into the cult of celluloid celebrity and appears to have his feet firmly on the ground.
As a child, he moved house 15 times in Britain and Ireland as his bohemian parents constantly sought new challenges.
His mother Jini gave Ralph, the eldest of six children, a toy theatre to play with when he was just seven.
Jini, a writer and painter, was a towering influence on him. She died of breast cancer but not before she was taken by wheelchair to a private showing of "Schindler's List."
OSCAR NOMINATION FOR "SCHINDLER'S LIST"
Fiennes graduated in 1985 from the prestigious Royal Academy of Dramatic Arts where students dubbed him "The Voice Beautiful".

Next came The Open Air Theatre in London's Regent's Park followed by a stint as the rising star of the Royal Shakespeare Company. His fortunes changed dramatically when Spielberg spotted him playing Heathcliff in a film version of "Wuthering Heights".
That opened the door to "Schindler's List" which won Fiennes an Oscar nomination as Best Supporting Actor.
Critics say he was lucky not to win and be forever condemned to the bad guy role that first brought him international fame.
The tortured soul is now ready to lighten up after the stage rigours of playing an agonised Russian landowner who falls out of love with his wife -- and life -- in "Ivanov".
For his next screen role he is to recreate the suave hero of the cult television series "The Avengers".
"I am looking forward to it very much -- the umbrella, the pinstripe suit, the vintage Jaguar," he said with relish. ($1=.6228 Pound)
